title: Debt
intro: Debt begins with an ordinary deadline: the year is ending and money is needed. It grows into a fantasy of confrontation, punishment and death, but keeps returning to the practical demand to be paid. That return matters. Revenge cannot settle the account that started the song. Along the way, money owed expands into favours owed, so the dispute is also about time, effort and recognition: why does another person's convenience count for more than the work that made this money possible?
reading: Material need escalates into revenge that cannot satisfy the original need; financial and emotional ledgers overlap.

revisions.7-year-end: The year-end deadline gives the anger a material starting point. He is not initially boasting about having money; he needs money that somebody else is keeping from him. Repetition turns 'must have money' into a pressure that cannot be talked away. Remember this opening when the song becomes extravagantly violent: the speaker's fantasy grows enormous, while the original problem remains embarrassingly simple and unresolved.
revisions.phrase-7-work: The important word is 'either': earning this money was not easy for him either. For a moment he appeals to a shared understanding of labour, rather than threatening punishment. The debtor is being asked to recognise the person whose effort sits behind the sum. That recognition is what the earlier insults cannot secure. Having to spend still more time chasing payment compounds the original loss.
revisions.7-favors-owed: A favour debt has no agreed price or repayment date. By adding it to the daily business of collecting money, he makes relationships feel like accounts that never close. The grievance broadens from one unpaid sum to a pattern of giving more than he receives. It also reveals the trap in the speaker's position: if every slight becomes another outstanding balance, he cannot stop doing the work of remembering and collecting.
revisions.editorial-7-dream: Calling the imagined death a dream come true is the point where repayment gives way to annihilation. Yet the song soon demands the money back again. A dead debtor cannot satisfy that demand. The clash makes the revenge sequence read as an outlet for powerless anger, rather than a workable solution to it. The ending returns us to the same year-end need; the fantasy has changed the scale of the language without settling anything.
